assignments.title: Critical Questions: Hamilton and Jefferson on the National Bank (1791)
assignments.html:
Read the primary source for this week: the opinions Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton wrote for President Washington about the national bank. Then answer both questions in your own words. Aim for four to six sentences each.

  1. Both men are reading the same Constitution, but they follow different rules for deciding what Congress is allowed to do. Without copying their words, explain the rule each man is using, and tell which rule leaves Congress with more room to act.
  2. Washington read both opinions and then signed the bank bill. Explain why this decision mattered for Americans who lived long after 1791, not just for the government in that year.

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

assignments.title: Primary Source Exercise: The Alien and Sedition Acts (1798)
assignments.html:
Read the Alien and Sedition Acts. Then answer both questions in your own words, in four to six sentences each.

  1. The Sedition Act made it a crime to publish "false" writing against the government. The Federalists said they were punishing lies, not free speech. What idea about free speech were they relying on, and why would that idea be hard to use fairly when the country is afraid of war?
  2. Jefferson and Madison answered the Acts with the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions. Why might their idea, that a state can judge a federal law for itself, matter for the United States long after 1798?

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

assignments.title: Critical Questions: Jefferson's First Inaugural Address (1801)
assignments.html:
Read the primary source for this week: Thomas Jefferson's First Inaugural Address. Then answer both questions in your own words. Aim for four to six sentences each.

  1. Jefferson spoke to a country that had just come through a tie, 36 votes, and talk of force. Suppose his speech had attacked the Federalists as enemies of the republic instead of calling them fellow citizens. What might have happened next, and why?
  2. Why would later Americans care about a speech in which the winner of a bitter election speaks to the losers as part of the same nation? Explain why it matters beyond the year 1801.

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

assignments.html:

  1. Suppose Marshall had ordered Madison to deliver Marbury's commission. What would Jefferson likely have done, and what would that have meant for the Court?
  2. Why does the power Marshall claimed in this opinion matter to ordinary Americans today, not just to the government in 1803?

assignments.title: Quarter 3 Capstone: Crossroads, A Turning-Point Dossier
assignments.html:
What you are doing

All quarter you have followed a young republic as it made choices about money, land, power, and freedom. Each choice settled one question and opened a bigger one. For this Capstone you will pick one turning point and build a dossier about it: a short, organized Word document that explains what happened, shows how it could have gone another way, and traces what it left unresolved.

Choose one turning point

  • Hamilton's plan for the national bank and the debt (Lesson F.1)
  • The Alien and Sedition Acts and the election of 1800 (Lessons F.2 and F.3)
  • Marbury v. Madison and McCulloch v. Maryland (Lesson F.4)
  • The Louisiana Purchase (Lesson 1.1)
  • The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine (Lesson 1.2)
  • Clay's American System (Lesson 1.3)
  • Indian removal under Jackson (Lesson 1.4)
  • The Missouri Compromise (Lesson 4.1)
  • The Nullification Crisis (Lesson 4.2)
  • The annexation of Texas and the Mexican War (Lessons 3.4 and 4.3)

What your dossier must include (700 to 1,000 words, plus the table)

  1. The Situation (about 150 words). What problem did leaders face, and who wanted what?
  2. The Decision (about 200 words). What did they do, and why? Name at least two people and what each one argued.
  3. A Timeline Table. A Word table with at least five rows (Date, Event, Why it mattered).
  4. Two Sources. Quote or closely describe two primary sources from this quarter's lessons or Primary Source pages. For each, say who wrote it, for whom, and what it can and cannot tell us.
  5. The Road Not Taken (about 200 words). Pick one point where a different choice was truly possible. What might have happened, and what would have made it hard?
  6. What It Left Unresolved (about 150 words). What question did this turning point leave open that a later generation had to face?
  7. What I Am Still Unsure About (2 to 3 sentences). Name something the sources cannot settle or where historians disagree.

Working alone or in a group

You can work alone. If you chose "Yes" to group work in your Module Intro, you may team up with one or two classmates and submit one shared dossier. A group of two adds 300 words; a group of three adds 500. Put every member's name at the top. Each member also writes a 2 to 3 sentence note at the end saying what they contributed. Group members are scored with the same rubric. One member submits the file for the group.

M365 Skill Step

Name your file LastName_FirstName_Q3Capstone_HIS7 (a group uses the submitter's name and adds the other last names, such as LastName_FirstName_Q3Capstone_HIS7_Group). Save it in your Optima → History → HIS7_2026-27 folder in OneDrive, then upload it here with Submit Assignment, then File Upload.

M365 Skill You're Practicing: Inserting and Formatting a Table (Word). Use Insert, then Table, for your timeline. Apply a Heading 1 style to each section title.

Your teacher will score your Capstone with the rubric attached to this assignment: understanding of the material, quality of reasoning, clarity and precision of expression, and intellectual honesty.

assignments.title: Critical Questions: The Emancipation Proclamation (1863)
assignments.html:

assignments.title: Quarter 4 Capstone: Point of No Return, A Case File on the Union Tested
assignments.html:
What you are doing

Historians argue about when the Union could no longer have been saved by compromise, and about what the war and Reconstruction actually settled. For this Capstone you will act as an investigator. You will pick three moments between 1850 and 1877, build a case file in Word, and then argue for which moment was the real point of no return.

Choose three moments (from different stages: at least one before the war, one during it, and one after it)

  • Before: the Compromise of 1850 and Fugitive Slave Act (Lessons 4.4, 5.1), the Kansas-Nebraska Act (5.2), Dred Scott and the Lincoln-Douglas debates (5.3), John Brown's raid (5.4), the secession of the Lower South (5.5)
  • During: Fort Sumter (6.1), the Emancipation Proclamation (6.4), Vicksburg and Gettysburg (6.5), Sherman's march (6.7), Lee's surrender (6.8)
  • After: Johnson's plan (7.1), the Fourteenth Amendment (7.2), freedpeople's new lives (7.3), the end of Reconstruction in 1877 (7.4)

What your case file must include (800 to 1,100 words, plus the table)

  1. Three Exhibits (about 150 words each). For each moment: what happened, who decided, and what the choice was. Give one quotation or detail from a lesson or source for each.
  2. A Timeline Table. At least six rows (Date, Event, What changed).
  3. Could It Have Gone Otherwise? (about 150 words, for one exhibit). What might have happened with a different choice, and what would have made it hard?
  4. Your Verdict (about 200 words). Which of your three moments was the real point of no return, the moment after which the outcome could not be changed? Defend your choice with at least two pieces of evidence. Then say what the strongest argument for a different moment would be.
  5. What the War Settled and What It Left Unresolved (about 100 words). Name one thing settled and one thing left open by 1877.
  6. What I Am Still Unsure About (2 to 3 sentences). Name something the evidence cannot settle.

Working alone or in a group

Same rules as before: solo, or one shared file for a group of two or three who opted in. A group of two adds 300 words; a group of three adds 500. Every member's name goes at the top, and each member adds a 2 to 3 sentence note on their contribution. Same rubric, one submitter.

Name your file LastName_FirstName_Q4Capstone_HIS7 (group: add _Group). Save it in your Optima → History → HIS7_2026-27 folder in OneDrive and upload it here with Submit Assignment, then File Upload.

M365 Skill You're Practicing: Inserting Footnotes (Word). Add at least two footnotes (References tab, then Insert Footnote) to cite your quotations by lesson or source title.

Your teacher will score your Capstone with the rubric attached to this assignment: understanding of the material, quality of reasoning, clarity and precision of expression, and intellectual honesty.

quizzes.description: This quiz covers Lesson F.1 and Lesson F.2. You may take it twice, and your higher score counts. Some questions ask you to put two or more facts together, so think before you answer.

questions.text: Virginia had already paid most of its war debts by 1790. Based on this, which reaction to Hamilton's assumption plan would you expect from many Virginians?

answers.text: They would welcome it, because it would lower their taxes to nothing.
They would ignore it, because it affected only the national government.

questions.text: In 1794, farmers in western Pennsylvania attacked tax collectors. Which fact about their lives best explains why the whiskey tax hurt them more than most Americans?

answers.text: Hauling grain over the mountains cost too much, so they turned it into whiskey, which they also used like money.
They were mostly bankers who owned shares in the Bank of the United States.
They had fought for Britain in the Revolution and were taxed as a punishment.

questions.text: Hamilton admitted the Constitution never mentions a national bank, yet he said Congress could create one. Which idea did his argument depend on?

answers.text: The President may do anything that Congress has not forbidden.
The states had agreed to let Congress copy the banks of Britain.
The Bill of Rights lets citizens vote on any new government agency.
Congress may use powers not listed if they help carry out powers that are listed.

questions.text: In 1793, a merchant whose business depended on trade with Britain would most likely have supported which group, and why?

answers.text: Republicans, because they sympathized with Britain.
Federalists, because Hamilton and his friends favored Britain, the nation's biggest trading partner.
Republicans, because Jefferson wanted the Bank to help merchants.
Neither group, because Washington's neutrality banned all trade with Britain.

questions.text: Jefferson and Madison believed the Sedition Act broke the Constitution, but they did not take the question to the Supreme Court. What was the best reason?

answers.text: The Supreme Court had not yet been created.
The Constitution forbids the Court from hearing laws about speech.
Jefferson was afraid that Washington would overrule the Court.
The Court was full of Federalists, so they expected it to side with the law.

questions.text: Which person would have been most likely to be charged under the Sedition Act of 1798?

answers.text: A Republican newspaper editor who wrote harsh attacks on President Adams.
A Federalist newspaper editor who praised President Adams.
A French diplomat who refused to pay a bribe.
A sailor who criticized the British navy in a letter to his family.

questions.text: The fight over the Bank (Lesson F.1) and the fight over the Sedition Act (Lesson F.2) were different disputes. What question lay underneath both of them?

answers.text: Which party had more members in Congress?
Whether the nation should side with Britain or France.
How much power the Constitution really gives the federal government.
Whether Washington should serve a third term.

questions.text: In the election of 1800 the Republicans clearly wanted Jefferson to be President, yet Jefferson and Burr tied with 73 votes each. What caused the tie?

answers.text: Several Federalist electors voted for Burr to confuse the count.
Electors cast two votes with no separate vote for Vice President, and every Republican elector voted for both men.
The House of Representatives had already voted and could not agree.
Burr refused to accept the Vice Presidency and asked for a recount.

questions.text: Hamilton disliked Jefferson's ideas, yet he urged Federalists in the House to support Jefferson over Burr. Which reason best explains his choice?

answers.text: He hoped Jefferson would bring back the whiskey tax.
He had promised Adams that he would help Jefferson win.

questions.text: The three-fifths compromise was a formula for dividing up House seats and taxes among the states. How did it matter to the election of 1800?

answers.text: It added seats and electors to the slaveholding states, which may have helped Jefferson defeat Adams.

It let each state decide whether to count its free citizens.

questions.text: In Marbury v. Madison, Marbury did not get his commission, yet people say Marshall won the larger fight. Why?

answers.text: He forced Madison to deliver every commission Adams had signed.
He convinced Jefferson to pardon the midnight judges.
He gave up a small power but claimed judicial review, the power to say a law is unconstitutional.
He ruled that the Supreme Court could be overruled by the President.

questions.text: Jefferson did not like the way Marshall's Court claimed the final word on the Constitution. Which belief would Jefferson most likely have held?

answers.text: Only state governors can decide what the Constitution allows.
Each branch of government, not just the Court, can judge what the Constitution allows.
The Constitution should not be explained by anyone after it is ratified.
The Supreme Court should be abolished and replaced by Congress.

questions.text: Maryland tried to tax the Baltimore branch of the Bank of the United States. Using Marshall's reasoning in McCulloch v. Maryland, why would that tax fail?

answers.text: Banks are never allowed to be taxed.
The Bank was owned by Maryland's own citizens.
Congress had no power to create the Bank in the first place.
The power to tax can become the power to destroy, and federal law is supreme over state law.

questions.text: A merchant in 1824 wants to ship goods by steamboat from New Jersey to New York. Which result of Gibbons v. Ogden helps the merchant most?

answers.text: Each state may now set its own steamboat rules.
Only New York may license steamboats on its waters.
Congress controls trade between the states, so one set of federal rules replaces many state rules.
Steamboats are not considered part of commerce.

questions.text: Some Republicans thought Lincoln's ten percent plan was too easy on the South. Which fact explains their view?

questions.text: Which set of events best explains why Northern support for Reconstruction faded in the 1870s?

questions.text: How did the disputed election of 1876 lead to the end of Reconstruction?

answers.text: Tilden won and removed the troops himself.

quizzes.title: Quarter 4 Exam: Compromise Fails and the Union Is Tested
quizzes.description: This exam covers Quarter 4 only: Lesson 4.4 through Module 7. It has 27 multiple-choice questions, one point each, and should take about 40 minutes. Read every question and all four answers before you choose. Many questions ask you to put two or more facts together, so think before you answer.

questions.text: The Wilmot Proviso, which banned slavery from land taken from Mexico, passed the House several times but always died in the Senate. Which fact best explains why?

answers.text: The Senate had no members from the free states, so the bill had no support there.
The Senate was evenly split between 15 free states and 15 slave states, so neither side could pass its way.
The President vetoed it each time it passed the House, and the veto was never overridden.
Its text would have banned slavery in the Southern states, which the Senate rejected.

questions.text: Douglas split Clay's failed bill into five separate bills and passed all five by September 1850. Why did that work?

answers.text: Each separate bill needed only a handful of votes to pass the Senate.
President Fillmore ordered the Senate to pass each of the five bills.
Separate bills did not need to be passed by the House of Representatives.
Members who opposed the whole package could still vote for the parts they liked.

questions.text: Southerners had once argued that a state could refuse to obey a federal law it thought unconstitutional. Why did Northern "personal liberty laws" against the Fugitive Slave Act make the South distrust any compromise?

answers.text: The North was now picking which federal laws to obey, so Southerners doubted it would honor any deal.
Southerners feared the North would stop buying Southern cotton and ruin its planters.
Southerners feared Northern states would send armed soldiers across the border into the South.
Southerners feared the Supreme Court would soon side with the North on every question.

questions.text: Southern senators would not vote to organize Kansas and Nebraska unless a change was made. What was the change, and what did it help bring about?

answers.text: The ban on slavery was extended to Kansas, and the Whig Party grew stronger.
Congress ended the Fugitive Slave Act, and the Free Soil Party disappeared.
The ban on slavery north of 36°30′ was repealed, and angry Northerners formed the Republican Party.
The railroad plan was cancelled, and the Democrats split in two.

questions.text: Taney's opinion in Dred Scott said Congress had no power to ban slavery in the territories. Why did Republicans say the decision made their whole program illegal?

answers.text: Their main goal was to end slavery in every state at once.
Their main goal was to make Dred Scott a citizen.
Their main goal was to keep slavery out of the territories.
Their main goal was to give the Supreme Court more power.

questions.text: Douglas's Freeport answer helped him win in Illinois. Why did it hurt him with Southern Democrats?

answers.text: It seemed to say that settlers could ignore the Court's ruling by refusing to pass laws that protect slavery.
Their main goal was to end slavery in every state of the Union at once.
Their main goal was to win Dred Scott his citizenship through a new court case.
Their main goal was to give the Supreme Court more power over the territories.

questions.text: Frederick Douglass told John Brown that Harpers Ferry was a trap. Which result of the raid showed Douglass was right?

answers.text: Lee's Marines drove Brown's men out, and the slaves rose in the mountains.
Brown escaped to Canada with the stolen weapons.
Virginia freed Brown after Northern leaders protested.
Brown's men were trapped in the fire engine house and captured, and the slaves did not rise.

questions.text: Lincoln won the election of 1860 with only about 40 percent of the popular vote. How did he still win the presidency?

answers.text: Southern states allowed his name on their ballots and counted every vote he received.
He carried every Northern state, and the Democrats had split their vote between two candidates.
The House of Representatives chose him after the electoral vote ended in a tie.
The Constitutional Union Party withdrew from the race and urged its voters to back him.

questions.text: Florida troops seized the arsenal at Chattahoochee and the forts at St. Augustine, but Union soldiers kept Fort Pickens, Key West, and the Dry Tortugas. Why did those forts matter later in the war?

answers.text: They gave the Union Navy bases on Florida's coast for the blockade.
They protected the railroad that carried Florida's cattle to Virginia.
They were the only place where Black soldiers could enlist.
They blocked the Union from ever reaching Georgia.

questions.text: Lincoln sent ships carrying only food to Fort Sumter and told South Carolina's governor they were coming. What was his thinking?

answers.text: It would force the soldiers inside the fort to surrender as soon as they had eaten.
It would show the Confederacy that the Union Navy was too weak to fight a war.
It would trick the Confederates into leaving Charleston Harbor without a fight.
It left Davis to decide whether to fire first, so the Confederacy would be the one to start a war.

questions.text: Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Arkansas refused to leave the Union until April 1861. What changed their minds?

answers.text: Lincoln announced that slavery would end in every state, including their own.
Lincoln asked them to send troops against their neighbors in the Confederacy.
Davis offered them important places in the new Confederate government.
The Supreme Court ruled that a state had the legal right to secede.

questions.text: Why did the smaller Confederate army keep beating the larger Union army in Virginia in 1862?

answers.text: Lee had many more soldiers and far more weapons than McClellan did.
McClellan refused to follow Lincoln's orders and retreated without being attacked.
Lee took bold risks and trusted his officers, while McClellan feared losing his army more than winning.
Jackson's army was larger than all of the Union forces in the East put together.

questions.text: When critics wanted Grant removed after Shiloh, Lincoln said, "I can't spare this man. He fights." Which problem in the East did this remark answer?

answers.text: Lee's refusal to cross the Potomac into the state of Maryland.
Pope's decision to retreat from the supply base at Manassas.
Jackson's long march through the Shenandoah Valley in the spring.
McClellan's habit of not attacking even when his army was larger.

questions.text: Secretary of State Seward told Lincoln to wait for a Union victory before announcing the Emancipation Proclamation. Why?

answers.text: Because the Constitution required a victory first.
If it came during a defeat, it would look like a cry for help.
Because Congress had not yet passed the Confiscation Acts.
Because the border states would not hear it before then.

questions.text: The Emancipation Proclamation freed slaves only in states still in rebellion. Which reason did Lincoln give that explains this limit?

answers.text: Lincoln believed Congress would end slavery in the border states during the following year.
Lincoln thought the Constitution allowed him to free slaves only inside the Deep South.
It was a war measure against property that helped the enemy, so it did not reach loyal border states.
Lincoln wanted slavery to continue in the border states for as long as the war lasted.

questions.text: On July 3-4, 1863, Pickett's Charge failed and Vicksburg surrendered. What did these two events do together?

answers.text: They ended Lee's hope of winning by invading the North and cut the Confederacy in two along the Mississippi.
They ended the war within weeks, because Lee and Davis agreed to make peace.
They gave the Confederacy control of the whole length of the Mississippi River.
They persuaded Britain and France to recognize the Confederacy as a nation.

questions.text: In 1863 a poor laborer and a rich merchant in New York both received draft notices. Which man was more likely to avoid service, and why?

answers.text: The laborer, because the draft excused men who owned no property.
The merchant, because he could pay $300 or hire a substitute.
The merchant, because the draft excused men over thirty.
Neither, because the Union draft allowed no exceptions.

questions.text: Black regiments, including the 54th Massachusetts, fought at Olustee in 1864. Which earlier change made it possible for Black men to serve in the Union army?

answers.text: The Homestead Act, which gave land to soldiers.
The Thirteenth Amendment, which ended slavery.
The Union draft, which required Black men to serve.
The Emancipation Proclamation, after which Black men could join.

questions.text: In six weeks of fighting, Grant lost about 55,000 men and Lee about 33,000, yet Grant kept attacking. Why was this a sound plan?

answers.text: The Union could replace its soldiers and the Confederacy could not.
Grant believed Lee would surrender after the first heavy losses.
Grant's army was smaller and had to attack before Lee grew stronger.
Lincoln had ordered him not to stop fighting for any reason.

questions.text: Lincoln believed in the summer of 1864 that he would probably lose the election. Why did the fall of Atlanta help him win?

answers.text: It forced McClellan to withdraw from the race for President that November.
It ended the war, so voters felt they no longer needed a change in leaders.
It showed voters that the war was being won, which ended the weariness that had made them doubt it.
It convinced a large number of Southern voters to support Lincoln in the election.

questions.text: Some of Lee's officers urged him to scatter his army and fight on as guerrillas. Why did it matter that Lee refused?

answers.text: Lee's army was too large to hide in the mountains.
Grant had promised to hang every officer who kept fighting.
A guerrilla war might have dragged on for years and left much deeper hatred.
Guerrilla fighters were not allowed to sign a parole.

questions.text: Mississippi's Black Code let freedpeople marry, own some property, and sue in court, but required yearly labor contracts and fined people without work. What aim did the codes share?

answers.text: To give freedpeople the same rights as white citizens.
To pay for new schools in the South.
To help the Freedmen's Bureau find work for former soldiers.
To keep a steady supply of workers for white landowners.

questions.text: The Fourteenth Amendment says each state's seats in Congress depend on its whole population, and a state that kept men from voting would lose seats. Why would this give Southern states a reason to let Black men vote?

answers.text: Black voters would pay higher taxes to the state.
Keeping Black men from voting would lower the state's number of seats in Congress.
The amendment ordered every state to hold a new election.
Southern states would lose their seats if they refused to ratify it.

questions.text: Which choice correctly compares Florida's constitutions of 1838 and 1868?

answers.text: The 1838 constitution protected slavery and let only free white men vote, but the 1868 one let all adult male citizens vote and made everyone equal before the law.
The 1838 constitution let all adult male citizens vote regardless of race, but the 1868 one let only free white men vote.
Both constitutions protected slavery, but the 1868 one also set up a system of public schools for the state.
Both constitutions let every man vote, but the 1868 one gave the governor strong powers over county officials.

questions.text: Many sharecroppers bought seed, tools, and food on credit before the crop came in. Why did so many end the year owing more than they earned?

answers.text: Landowners charged them more in rent each year than the whole crop was worth.
If the crop failed or prices fell, they could not pay the store debt, and it carried over to the next year.
They were paid in paper money that lost its value before they could spend it.
The Freedmen's Bureau charged them a fee for every labor contract they signed.

questions.text: Grant's Enforcement Acts and troops broke up the Klan for a time, yet federal protection of Black voters soon faded. Which pair of events best explains the change?

answers.text: The Supreme Court narrowed federal power in Cruikshank, and Northerners tired of the struggle after the Panic of 1873.
Congress repealed the Fourteenth Amendment, and Grant resigned from the presidency in disgrace.
The Supreme Court banned the Klan, and Southern voters elected Black governors in every state.
The Freedmen's Bureau closed its offices, and Congress then passed the Fifteenth Amendment.

questions.text: Which statement best describes what the Civil War settled and what it left unsettled?

answers.text: It settled that the Court alone decides the meaning of the Constitution, but left slavery in the border states.
It settled that Congress could not override a veto, but left the question of the Union open.
It settled that the amendments would be strictly enforced, but left the states free to leave.
It settled that no state could leave the Union, but how far the new amendments would be enforced stayed open.

questions.text: Which idea from these lessons, or from the whole semester, is still unclear to you? It might be sharecropping, the Enforcement Acts, the Redeemers, the Compromise of 1877, or how the compromises of the 1800s led to the Civil War. Say what you do not yet understand.

Many Black Southerners kept voting and serving in office during Reconstruction even though the Klan threatened them. Which of these virtues did that require: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, or responsibility? Explain in two or three sentences, and tell about a time you needed that same virtue.

discussions.title: Discussion: Hamilton vs. Jefferson, How Much Power Does the Constitution Give the Federal Government?
discussions.html:
Pick one side. Make one specific claim about how much power the Constitution gives the federal government. You may defend Hamilton's reading (Congress may use powers that help carry out its listed powers) or Jefferson's reading (Congress may use only the powers the Constitution lists). Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or primary sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then do two things:

  1. Reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.
  2. Connect to today. In one or two sentences, name one decision the federal government makes today that people still argue about, and say which man's reading the people on one side of that argument seem to follow.

discussions.title: Discussion: Why Is the Election of 1800 Called a Revolution?
discussions.html:
Thomas Jefferson later called the election of 1800 a revolution, yet no one was killed and no government was overthrown. Make one specific claim about what, if anything, was truly revolutionary about it. Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Tecumseh's Confederacy and the Road to the War of 1812
discussions.html:
Historians disagree about what pushed the United States into war in 1812. Some stress British seizure of American sailors at sea. Others stress trouble on the frontier, where Tecumseh and the Native confederacy were seen as a threat backed by Britain. Make one specific claim about which cause mattered more, or whether the two were really one story. Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Was Jackson's Election a Triumph for Democracy?
discussions.html:
Jackson's election in 1828 brought far more voters to the polls and made the presidency a voice for ordinary men. His years in office also saw Indian removal and the loss of the vote for some free Black men. Make one specific claim: was Jackson's election a triumph for democracy, a mixed result, or something else? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Lowell Mills, Opportunity or Exploitation?
discussions.html:
The Lowell mills gave young farm women wages of their own, a place to live, and a chance to leave the farm. They also meant twelve or thirteen hour days, loud machines, and lint-filled air. Make one specific claim: were the Lowell mills mainly an opportunity, mainly exploitation, or both? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Jefferson's Dilemma, Holding "a Wolf by the Ear"
discussions.html:
Jefferson called slavery "a wolf by the ear": wrong to hold, but dangerous to let go. Historians disagree about whether Jefferson and Madison could have found a safe way to end slavery, or whether they simply did not try hard enough. Make one specific claim about which view the evidence supports better. Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Calhoun's "Positive Good," Why Did the South's Argument Change?
discussions.html:
In Jefferson's time many Southern leaders called slavery a wrong they did not know how to end. By the 1830s Calhoun called it a positive good. Make one specific claim about which cause mattered most in that change: the profits of cotton, the fear after Nat Turner's revolt, the growth of the abolitionist movement, or something else. Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Jefferson's "Fire Bell in the Night," Why Did Missouri Alarm Him?
discussions.html:
Most Americans were glad when the Missouri Compromise passed. Jefferson heard "a fire bell in the night" and called it the knell of the Union. Make one specific claim: was Jefferson right that the compromise only postponed the fight, or was it a wise way to keep the peace for thirty years? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Nullification, Can a State Overrule the Union?
discussions.html:
South Carolina said a state could declare a federal law void inside its borders. Jackson said that disunion by armed force is treason. Make one specific claim: can a single state overrule the federal government? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then do two things:

  1. Reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.
  2. Connect to today. Look for a news story about a state and the federal government disagreeing over a law, a tax, or a program. In one or two sentences, say how it is like or unlike the nullification crisis.

discussions.title: Discussion: Webster's Seventh of March Speech, Statesmanship or Surrender?
discussions.html:
Webster supported the Compromise of 1850, including the Fugitive Slave Act, to keep the Union together. Many people in his own region called it a surrender. Make one specific claim: was his speech an act of statesmanship, a surrender, or something in between? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Dred Scott, Can the Court Settle What Congress Cannot?
discussions.html:
Many Americans hoped the Supreme Court could end the argument over slavery in the territories. Instead, the Dred Scott decision made the fight worse. Make one specific claim: can a court settle a question that the elected branches cannot? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: John Brown, Martyr, Terrorist, or Prophet?
discussions.html:
Historians still disagree about John Brown. Some call him a martyr, some a terrorist, some a prophet. Make one specific claim about which description fits him best, or explain why none of them does. Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources, such as what he said or what he actually did, to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Why Did the Upper South Wait?
discussions.html:
Seven states left the Union before Fort Sumter. Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Arkansas waited until Lincoln called for troops, and four border states never left. Make one specific claim about the main reason the Upper South waited, and what Lincoln's call for 75,000 militia changed. Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Why Did Lincoln Wait to Free the Slaves?
discussions.html:
When the war began, Lincoln said he fought to save the Union. He did not announce the Emancipation Proclamation until almost two years later. Make one specific claim: was Lincoln wise to wait, did he wait too long, or was waiting the only choice he had? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: What Did Lincoln Mean by "a New Birth of Freedom"?
discussions.html:
At Gettysburg, Lincoln said that the nation would have "a new birth of freedom." Make one specific claim about what he meant: freedom for the slaves, a renewed Union, a new understanding of the Declaration of Independence, or something else. Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Was Sherman's March Justified?
discussions.html:
Sherman believed in total war and said that "war is cruelty, and you cannot refine it." His soldiers destroyed railroads, took crops, and burned barns, mills, and cotton gins, but did not usually kill civilians. Make one specific claim: was Sherman's March justified, unjustified, or justified only in part? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources, including what Sherman did, what he did not do, and what he was trying to accomplish, to back your claim. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Was the Fourteenth Amendment a Revolution?
discussions.html:
The Fourteenth Amendment changed who counted as a citizen and what states could do. Some say it was a revolution. Others say its promise depended on enforcement that soon faded. Make one specific claim: was the Fourteenth Amendment a revolution, a promise that was only partly kept, or something else? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then do two things:

  1. Reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.
  2. Connect to today. Find a current news story that mentions the Fourteenth Amendment. In one or two sentences, say what right is being argued about and how it is like or unlike the problems of 1866.

discussions.title: Discussion: What Did the Civil War Settle, and What Did It Leave Unresolved?
discussions.html:
This is the question that ties the whole course together. Look back at the compromises and crises you have studied, from Washington's warning about party spirit to the end of Reconstruction. The war settled that no state could leave the Union, and it ended slavery. It left other questions open. Make one specific claim about the most important thing the war settled, or the most important question it left unresolved. Use at least one fact from these lessons or from earlier in the course to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.
